title: Perfume and silver (Mark 14:1–11)
hook: a woman anoints him with costly nard; Judas goes to the priests
carry: she has done a beautiful thing

segments.voice: Yesterday, a doorkeeper and a single word. Your line was watch. Today the last part of Mark begins: the passion and the empty tomb.

Two days before the Passover. In Jerusalem, the chief priests and scribes want a quiet way to arrest Jesus, but not during the feast, they say, or the people will riot. Out in the village of Bethany, Jesus is at dinner in the house of a man called Simon the leper. A woman comes in carrying an alabaster jar of perfume, pure nard, very expensive. She doesn't dab a little. She breaks the jar and pours the whole thing over his head. The smell fills the house. Every conversation stops. Somebody is already doing the math.
screen: `TWO DAYS BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `AN ALABASTER JAR, BROKEN.` → `SOMEBODY DOES THE MATH.`

segments.voice: Some at the table are indignant. Why this waste? It could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor. And they scold her. Jesus says, in the King James Bible: "Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me." The Greek word for good there, kalos, also means beautiful. She has done a beautiful thing. Then: the poor you always have with you, and you can do them good whenever you want. He's echoing Moses, who said the poor shall never cease out of the land, and so, open your hand to them. In Deuteronomy, that line is a reason to give, not an excuse. Here it's about this moment: you will not always have me. She has done what she could, he says; she has anointed my body beforehand for burying. Remember the word Christ, the anointed one? Here, in Mark, someone anoints him at last, and he says it's for his burial. Wherever the good news is told in the whole world, he promises, what she has done will be told in memory of her. Yet Mark never tells us her name. John's Gospel, telling a similar scene, names her Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. Then Mark cuts sharply to someone he does name. Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the chief priests to hand him over. They're glad, and promise him money. Perfume poured out for love. Silver taken for a betrayal.
screen: `WHY THIS WASTE?` · `KALOS: GOOD, AND BEAUTIFUL.` · `ANOINTED FOR HIS BURIAL.` · `JUDAS GOES TO THE PRIESTS.` · then, large: `SHE HATH WROUGHT A GOOD WORK ON ME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you love, and what it would look like to do something extravagant for them: not practical, just beautiful, like a whole afternoon, a letter that takes an hour, or showing up in person when a text would do. Notice the voice that says what a waste, listen to it kindly, and picture doing it anyway. If you pray, offer that love to God too.
Kalos, the Greek word for good, which also means beautiful. A woman pours out costly nard for love, and Judas goes to take silver for a betrayal.
Your line: she has done a beautiful thing. And it's told in memory of her. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians often read this story at the start of Holy Week; many churches use anointing oil in baptism, confirmation or prayer for the sick, and Christians remember the unnamed woman as an example of extravagant devotion.

match.prompt: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
pairs: broke the jar and poured it

myth: Mark tells us the woman's name
Mark leaves her unnamed. John's similar scene names her Mary.
the onlookers priced the perfume at over three hundred denarii
"more than three hundred pence," in the King James. they wanted it sold for the poor.
Mark says Judas was paid thirty pieces of silver
Mark says only that they promised him money. thirty pieces is Matthew's detail.

fork.setup: you're at the table when a woman pours a whole jar of costly perfume over Jesus's head. the others are scolding her. what does Jesus say?
options: she should have sold it for the poor.
let her alone; she has done a beautiful thing.
fork.reveal: "Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me." and wherever the gospel is told, she will be remembered.

original.note: Greek: good, fine, beautiful. behind the King James "good work" in Mark 14:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus said the poor don't matter.
what it means: a woman's extravagant love anoints him for burial, and he says she has done a beautiful thing.
what a scholar hears: kalos means good and beautiful; the poor saying echoes Deuteronomy 15:11; and Mark sets her straight beside Judas.
recall: the right and the power to act

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): Cut unsourced numbers ("two miles", "about a year's wages", from teach, myth and fork) and "sealed" (Mark says she broke the box). Removed the unsourced history of the Mary Magdalene confusion ("Orthodox always kept them apart"), which needs a source to stand. "The only time anyone anoints him" softened. "It's never been permission to ignore the poor" recast as what Deuteronomy 15:11 says. "Sandwich" dropped here and in the trapdoor because day 207 builds its lesson on Mark's sandwiches. Myth reveal quotes KJV Mark 14:5 "more than three hundred pence".
Bethany 'two miles' from Jerusalem (John 11:18: fifteen furlongs); confirm.
Three hundred denarii 'about a year's wages' (a denarius being a day's wage). Confirm.

Mary Magdalene conflation: traced to Gregory the Great (591) in the Western church; the Orthodox kept them distinct; the Catholic calendar distinguished them after 1969. Confirm phrasing 'today the Catholic Church does too'.
'The only time anyone actually anoints him' in Mark: the women in 16:1 come to anoint but find the tomb empty. Confirm.
